mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Friday, October 9, 2026. Amazon announced it will stop using non-disclosure agreements, or NDAs, when negotiating data center deals with local governments. This policy change follows a similar move by Microsoft earlier this year and is intended to increase transparency regarding AI infrastructure projects. The secrecy surrounding these developments has previously fueled community opposition, leading to hundreds of moratoriums on new data centers in areas ranging from New York to San Francisco. By removing these restrictions, Amazon aims to address public concerns, though it remains to be seen how significantly this shift will alter the established processes for site selection and infrastructure deployment. In other infrastructure developments, AWS released a series of updates for AI builders, emphasizing the shift from merely selecting a model to managing the entire agentic system. The company announced that Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents, powered by OpenAI models, is now in public preview, allowing users to build production-ready agents that utilize AWS security, identity management, and audit tools. Additionally, AWS introduced a new open-source agent harness called Strands, which is designed to reduce token consumption by 28 percent, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model called Strands Decider that can perform tool selection and routing tasks locally with low latency. These updates are intended to help enterprises scale agents that can reason over private data while maintaining governance. A third major development concerns the management of GPU resources. The AI Infrastructure team at the Allen Institute for AI reported on its transition from a priority-based scheduler to a system centered on GPU time budgets and hierarchical fair-share allocation. The institute, which manages clusters of up to 1,024 NVIDIA GPUs for 150 researchers, faced significant challenges with a priority-based model, including "priority inflation"—where every task is labeled high-priority—and resource "squatting." By implementing a transparent administrative budgeting process, the team aims to improve the impact of their scheduling decisions and ensure that limited compute capacity is allocated more effectively across diverse research workloads. Regarding security and developer news, Sophos reported a 96 percent reduction in threat investigation time by utilizing OpenAI Daybreak, a program that helps integrate AI agents into cybersecurity workflows. Sophos noted that about 52 percent of its Managed Detection and Response cases are now handled end-to-end by these agents, which show an average response time of 89 seconds. Separately, developers are increasingly using frontier AI models combined with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to automate the creation of digital twins and simulation environments for robotics and autonomous driving. These tools allow developers to use natural language to direct AI agents in building physically accurate scenes, validating sensor outputs, and testing robot movements. In the realm of software integration, Postman detailed the architectural patterns used to implement its AI-native "Agent Mode" for 40 million developers. The company noted that integrating an agent into a mature, interface-driven product required moving beyond simple model and prompt tuning to address deeper challenges, such as controlling tool sprawl. Postman found that when an agent's available toolset exceeded 40, errors in tool selection and argument passing increased. To manage this, they implemented strict human-in-the-loop approvals for state-modifying actions and utilized Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to redact sensitive information before it reaches the language models. Finally, independent reporting highlights a growing trend of startups seeking access to sensitive user data, including inboxes and financial information, to power personal AI agents. This shift has prompted some companies, such as United, Apple, and Amazon, to implement restrictions against third-party agents accessing their platforms. Meanwhile, academic and safety researchers continue to debate the reliance on "refusal" as a primary safety mechanism. Experts note that teaching models to refuse harmful prompts is a probabilistic process that remains vulnerable to circumvention, raising questions about whether such safety measures can reliably prevent high-stakes outcomes like the development of biological pathogens.
